content: Approximately 30% of individuals with epilepsy in endemic regions are reported to have neurocysticercosis (NCC). This prevalence is consistent across both children and adults, supporting findings from southern Africa and India that NCC is a common cause of juvenile epilepsy. In Honduras, a clinical study revealed that 19% of epileptic patients had viable intracerebral cysticerci, while 65% exhibited calcifications consistent with NCC. Despite its frequency and severity, the societal and economic impacts of NCC remain poorly understood. Efforts are underway to assess the burden of NCC in endemic regions of Africa, Asia, and Latin America, as well as in countries with significant numbers of imported cases, such as the USA. Cysticercosis is becoming an increasing concern in developed countries due to the immigration of infected individuals from endemic areas. In 1993, the International Task Force for Disease Eradication declared cysticercosis eradicable based on its biological and transmission characteristics. However, eradication depends on behavioral changes in endemic populations and the implementation of appropriate biomedical control measures. The disease remains prevalent among impoverished populations due to factors such as the chronic nature of the infection, the variety of symptoms associated with NCC, limited awareness of the disease's burden and transmission, and the lack of field-applicable diagnostic tools. Despite the 1993 recommendation, cysticercosis/taeniasis has not been eliminated in any region, and no national control programs are in place. Advocacy efforts remain limited, even though regional working groups exist. The World Health Organization (WHO) has included cysticercosis/taeniasis in its Global Plan to Combat Neglected Tropical Diseases and in initiatives addressing zoonotic and marginalized infections. International epilepsy associations are increasingly recognizing NCC as a major preventable cause of epilepsy. Working groups have been formed to facilitate research and control efforts targeting Taenia solium infections. Two randomized controlled community trials have been conducted to evaluate strategies for controlling cysticercosis. In Peru, a trial involving nine villages assessed the impact of combined mass human and pig chemotherapy on the prevalence and incidence of porcine cysticercosis, showing some reduction in intervention villages compared to controls. In northern Tanzania, a trial in 42 villages demonstrated a 49% reduction in porcine cysticercosis incidence through improved pig management and educational programs. Predictive models suggest that long-term interventions focusing on sanitation and pig management are more effective than treating pigs or humans alone. The social consequences of NCC, primarily due to epileptic seizures, include stigmatization, isolation, and reduced work productivity. People with epilepsy often fail to receive appropriate treatment and face significant social disadvantages. For example, in West Cameroon, only 27% of individuals with epilepsy marry, and 39% fail to enter any professional activity. In Zambia, people with epilepsy experience poorer employment status, lower education levels, inadequate housing, and greater food insecurity. Adult females with epilepsy are more likely to deliver their babies at home and face a higher risk of sexual violence. Additionally, individuals with epilepsy are prone to accidents during seizures, such as burns, drowning, or injuries from automobile accidents, which further contribute to the burden of NCC. Disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) lost due to NCC are estimated to be higher than for some other neglected tropical diseases. WHO is currently calculating the global burden of NCC through a systematic review of the literature. Cystic echinococcosis (CE) and alveolar echinococcosis (AE) are caused by the larval stages of cestode tapeworms of the genus Echinococcus. The adult worms are found in carnivores, particularly dogs and foxes. Human CE, caused by Echinococcus granulosus, accounts for approximately 95% of the estimated 2–3 million global echinococcosis cases. CE and AE are emerging or re-emerging diseases of increasing public health concern. E. granulosus has a worldwide distribution, with high prevalence in regions such as Central Asia, China, the Mediterranean, Russia, and South America. CE is primarily transmitted through ingestion of material contaminated with dog feces containing E. granulosus eggs, leading to the development of hydatid cysts in the liver, lungs, or other organs. These cysts can grow over time, causing pressure symptoms, and may rupture, resulting in anaphylactic shock and death if untreated. Treatment for CE typically involves surgery or percutaneous drainage to relieve pressure symptoms, although these procedures carry risks such as cyst fluid spillage and anaphylaxis. High-dose albendazole, alone or in combination with praziquantel, is effective and can be used preoperatively to sterilize cysts. However, surgical and imaging resources are often unavailable in resource-poor settings. Preventive measures include avoiding contact with dog feces, improving sanitation, treating dogs with praziquantel, and health education. Successful campaigns have eliminated CE from island nations such as Cyprus, Iceland, and New Zealand. AE, caused by Echinococcus multilocularis, is found in the northern hemisphere, including Central Europe, northern and central Eurasia, and parts of North America. AE is a more severe disease with a high fatality rate and poor prognosis if untreated. The parasitic mass, primarily in the liver, infiltrates surrounding tissues and can metastasize to other organs. Radical surgery is the cornerstone of treatment but is rarely available in resource-poor populations. Long-term albendazole therapy has improved survival rates, but early diagnosis is crucial to reduce the need for radical surgery. Liver transplantation has been performed in some AE cases. Imaging methods such as ultrasound, CT, and MRI are essential for diagnosis but are often inaccessible in rural or impoverished areas. Portable ultrasound scanners now enable community-based surveys in endemic regions. Immunodiagnosis complements imaging for primary diagnosis and patient follow-up. Asian schistosomiasis, caused by Schistosoma japonicum and Schistosoma mekongi, is transmitted through contact with freshwater containing cercariae released from snails. Reservoir hosts include water buffalo, cattle, rodents, dogs, and pigs. In humans, S. japonicum is associated with liver disease, splenomegaly, bloody diarrhea, malnutrition, anemia, and cognitive impairment. Disability weights for S. japonicum are significantly higher than those used in global burden estimates. Control efforts should consider the varying contributions of animal reservoirs in different endemic areas.
